present.none: no present: لَيْسَ is itself the present negation (“is not”)

masdar.none: a frozen verb (only the past forms, meaning the present): it has no maṣdar

governs.what: the predicate, often with بِـ (لَيْسَ كَبِيرًا / لَيْسَ بِكَبِيرٍ)

contrasts.value: a sentence without a verb (is not); conjugated

profile.feeling: The “is not” of Arabic: a whole verb that only negates.

senses.def: is not, am not, are not — negates a sentence without a verb (present)

phrases.meaning: seeing for yourself is better than any report

synonyms.nuance: “non-, un-, other than” before a noun or adjective: غَيْرُ صَحِيحٍ = incorrect (a noun, not a verb)
negates a nominal sentence in classical style: مَا هٰذَا بَشَرًا (Qurʾān 12:31, “this is not a human being”)

etymology.text: Uncertain (Wiktionary): traditionally explained as a contraction of لَا “not” + an old existential أَيْس “there is”, which would be cognate with Hebrew יֵשׁ (yesh, “there is”) — or of an unexplained verb لَيِسَ.

funFacts: Arabic has no verb for “is” in the present — but it has one for “is not”.
pitfalls: Its predicate is accusative: هُوَ طَبِيبٌ → لَيْسَ طَبِيبًا.
It looks like a past verb (لَيْسَ، لَسْتُ، لَيْسُوا) but means the present: لَسْتُ جَائِعًا = I am not hungry.
To negate a present verb use لَا, not لَيْسَ: لَا أُحِبُّ (I don’t like).
subtleties: The stem shortens to las- before consonant endings: لَيْسَ but لَسْتُ، لَسْنَا، لَسْنَ.
It agrees with its subject: هٰذِهِ لَيْسَتْ جَزَرَةً (feminine), هٰذَا لَيْسَ بَصَلًا (masculine).

contrasts.value: a present verb; a prohibition with the jussive

profile.feeling: The workhorse negation of the present; also in many fixed phrases.

senses.def: no, not any — “there is no …” (لَا + a noun in -a without tanwīn: لَا شَكَّ); “I have no …” is لَيْسَ عِنْدِي …

examples.tr: There is no doubt about that.
There is no water in the house.

phrases.text: لَا يُلْدَغُ الْمُؤْمِنُ مِنْ جُحْرٍ وَاحِدٍ مَرَّتَيْنِ
phrases.tr: a believer is not stung from the same hole twice
phrases.meaning: a wise person does not fall for the same trick twice (a hadith used as a proverb)

synonyms.nuance: negates a sentence without a verb (“is not”), conjugated
negates the past, with the jussive: لَمْ آكُلْ (I didn’t eat)
negates the future, with the subjunctive: لَنْ آكُلَ (I won’t eat)
negates a past verb (also very common in the dialects): مَا أَكَلْتُ

etymology.text: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *lā; compare Hebrew לֹא (lo).

funFacts: Modern Arabic uses لَا like a prefix “non-, un-”: لَاسِلْكِيّ (wireless, lit. “no-wire-ish”).
pitfalls: لَا negates the present only. Past: لَمْ + jussive (لَمْ آكُلْ); future: لَنْ + subjunctive (لَنْ آكُلَ).
Written exactly like the answer لَا “no” — read the position: before a verb it means “not”.
subtleties: The verb after لَا stays indicative: لَا أُحِبُّ (-u); after لَا of prohibition it is jussive: لَا تَقْلَقْ (-∅).
لَا + noun = “there is no”: لَا شَكَّ — the noun takes -a without tanwīn.
“I have no car” is not said with لَا: لَيْسَ عِنْدِي سَيَّارَةٌ — the “no” goes on the verbless sentence (لَيْسَ).

contrasts.value: a past verb (literary in MSA, everyday in the dialects)

profile.feeling: The negation of the past in older and literary Arabic — and the everyday “not” of the spoken dialects.

senses.def: not — negates a past verb: مَا ذَهَبْتُ (I did not go); literary in MSA, everyday in the dialects

examples.tr: I didn’t go to work yesterday.
I have never seen anything like it.

synonyms.nuance: the standard negation of the past in MSA, with the jussive: لَمْ أَذْهَبْ

etymology.text: Wiktionary lists it as a particle meaning “not; never”, an entry of its own beside the pronoun مَا “what”.

funFacts: The dialects negate almost everything with مَا (Egyptian and Levantine مَا رُحْتِش / مَا رُحْت, “I didn’t go”), while MSA prefers لَمْ.
pitfalls: مَا + a past verb = not (مَا ذَهَبْتُ); مَا before a noun or in a question = what (مَا هٰذَا؟) — the word after it tells which.
subtleties: In MSA the neutral negation of the past is لَمْ + jussive (لَمْ أَذْهَبْ); مَا + past sounds literary or emphatic.

senses.def: nothing (as an answer, or “there is nothing …”)

examples.tr: What would you like? — Nothing, thanks.

synonyms.nuance: with a verb: لَا أُرِيدُ شَيْئًا = I don’t want anything

etymology.text: لَا (“not, no”) + شَيْء (“thing”) in the accusative without tanwīn, the form after the لَا that denies a whole kind (Wiktionary has both words).

funFacts: Built exactly like English “no-thing”: لَا + شَيْء.
pitfalls: With a verb, use لَا + verb + شَيْئًا: لَا أُرِيدُ شَيْئًا (I don’t want anything) — not *أُرِيدُ لَا شَيْءَ.
subtleties: شَيْءَ has -a without tanwīn: this is the لَا that denies a whole class (لَا النَّافِيَةُ لِلْجِنْسِ), as in لَا شَكَّ (no doubt).

profile.feeling: An empty room, a closed door: “nobody”.

examples.tr: Who is in the house? — Nobody.

examples.text: لَا أَحَدَ يَأْكُلُ اللَّحْمَ فِي بَيْتِنَا.
examples.tr: Nobody eats meat in our house.

synonyms.nuance: with a verb and an object: لَا أَرَى أَحَدًا = I don’t see anybody

etymology.text: لَا (“not, no”) + أَحَد (“one; someone, anyone”), related to وَاحِد (“one”) and cognate with Hebrew אֶחָד (ekhád, “one”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The same أَحَد is in أَحَدَ عَشَرَ (eleven, “one-ten”) and in الْأَحَد, Sunday, “day one” (Wiktionary).
pitfalls: As an object after a negated verb you need أَحَدًا: لَا أَرَى أَحَدًا (I don’t see anyone).
subtleties: After لَا أَحَدَ a verb can follow: لَا أَحَدَ يَأْكُلُ (nobody eats) — the verb is masculine singular.

meaningForms.none: the same forms in every meaning

examples.tr: Are you angry? — Not at all!

synonyms.nuance: never — only with a negated past: مَا رَأَيْتُهُ قَطُّ (I have never seen him)

funFacts: Literally “eternally”: the noun أَبَد is in إِلَى الْأَبَدِ, “forever”.
pitfalls: For “never” it needs a negation: لَا آكُلُ اللَّحْمَ أَبَدًا. Without one, in literary style, it means “forever”.
With a past verb use لَمْ … أَبَدًا or مَا … قَطُّ (later lessons), not لَا.
subtleties: It usually comes at the end of the sentence: لَا أَشْرَبُ الْقَهْوَةَ أَبَدًا.

contrasts.value: (not) even, (not) a single — after a negation

profile.feeling: Saying no to two things at once.

examples.tr: I drink neither tea nor coffee.
I have neither a brother nor a sister.
The child neither eats nor drinks.
He didn’t say a single word.

profile.synonymsNone: Arabic has no separate word: the normal negation of the sentence is repeated with وَ (وَلَا).
funFacts: Greek ούτε … ούτε and Russian ни … ни also repeat the negation; Arabic repeats it with “and”: وَلَا.
pitfalls: The first part is the normal negation of the sentence: لَا before a present verb, لَيْسَ in a sentence without a verb; only the second part is وَلَا.
subtleties: The nouns keep the case of their place: لَا أَشْرَبُ الشَّايَ وَلَا الْقَهْوَةَ (both accusative); لَيْسَ عِنْدِي أَخٌ وَلَا أُخْتٌ (both nominative).

plurals.note: things: a diptote, although it looks like أَفْعَال (grammarians disagree on its measure)

meaningForms.none: no other form belongs to one meaning (the plurals do: see plurals)

lexemes.role: thing, something; after a negated verb “anything”: لَا أُرِيدُ شَيْئًا = I don’t want anything. Needed for “nothing” with a verb.

profile.feeling: The all-purpose word: something, anything, everything.

examples.tr: I have lots of things in my bag.
I heard something in the kitchen.

phrases.tr: one thing is mentioned with another
phrases.meaning: that reminds me — said when one topic brings up another

synonyms.nuance: a matter, an affair (abstract), not a physical thing

etymology.text: A word of the root ش ي ء (Wiktionary), the root of شَاءَ, “to will, to want” (إِنْ شَاءَ اللّٰهُ); Wiktionary’s entry has no etymology section.

funFacts: شَيْء shares its root with شَاءَ, the “will” of إِنْ شَاءَ اللّٰهُ (God willing).
pitfalls: Accusative indefinite شَيْئًا: the hamza sits on a yāʾ seat (ئ) before the ending.
The plural أَشْيَاءُ is a diptote: no tanwīn.
subtleties: After a negated verb it means “anything”: لَا آكُلُ شَيْئًا (I’m not eating anything) — one negation, like English “not … anything”.
